alignment.note: The Vulgate reads 'Et respondens' (And answering) where Greek and Peshitta have 'And he asked' (καὶ ἐπηρώτησεν / ܘܡܫܐܠ). This represents a complete textual divergence, as the Vulgate transmits the response of a man from the crowd (v. 17) rather than Jesus' question to the scribes (v. 16).
Greek uses a simple aorist verb ἐπηρώτησεν; Peshitta employs the periphrastic construction ܡܫܐܠ ܗܘܐ (was asking) with the auxiliary verb ܗܘܐ, a common Syriac idiom for past progressive aspect.

Greek and Peshitta identify the addressees as 'the scribes' (γραμματεῖς / ܠܣܦܪܐ), while the Vulgate reads 'unus de turba' (one from the crowd), reflecting the textual divergence where the Vulgate transmits an entirely different verse.
Greek συζητεῖτε (disputing, debating) is rendered by Peshitta ܕܪܫܝܢ (seeking, inquiring), a semantic shift from contentious debate to neutral inquiry, though both convey questioning activity.
Peshitta adds the explicit subject pronoun ܐܢܬܘܢ (you), a common Syriac clarification where Greek relies on verbal inflection alone to indicate the second-person plural.

The Vulgate transmits entirely different content ('dixit: Magister, attuli filium meum ad te habentem spiritum mutum'), corresponding to Mark 9:17 rather than 9:16. This represents a verse-level textual divergence where the Vulgate witness conflates or substitutes verses.
